item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.

item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

item.content:encoded:
Cristopher Sánchez consigue su 18ma victoria, líder de MLB; Juan Soto se va de 4-1
El dominicano Cristopher Sánchez consiguió su 18.ª victoria, la mayor cantidad en las Grandes Ligas, para guiar la victoria el domingo 7-2 de los Filis de Filadelfia ante los Mets de Nueva York.
Los Filis (86-70), que rescataron un empate en la serie de cuatro juegos, llegaron al domingo en el tercer puesto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, a un juego de los Cachorros de Chicago y Padres de San Diego y con una ventaja de cuatro juegos sobre los Diamondbacks de Arizona.
Sánchez permitió seis hits —incluido el jonrón de Bo Bichette en la sexta entrada— y ponchó a seis en 6 1/3 innings, con lo que rompió el empate con Sonny Gray, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por el liderato de victorias en las Grandes Ligas.
El último lanzador de los Filis en liderar las mayores en victorias fue Steve Carlton, con 23 en 1982.
Justin Crawford conectó un triple de tres carreras y el venezolano Luis Arráez terminó con dos carreras impulsadas. Alec Bohm y Trea Turner aportaron cada uno un hit productor. Kyle Schwarber igualó su máximo de carrera con cuatro bases por bolas.
El novato Jonah Tong (2-2) permitió cuatro carreras y ponchó a cinco en 4 2/3 innings por los coleros Mets, que terminaron 36-45 en casa —su peor registro en Citi Field desde 2013, que fue de 33-48.
Los Mets atrajeron a 2.712.120 aficionados esta temporada, una caída de 5.870 aficionados por juego respecto a la temporada pasada —el descenso más pronunciado en las Grandes Ligas.
El dominicano Juan Soto bateó de 4-1.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.

Already have an account? Log in to continue.
Otherwise, follow the link below to join.
| Please log in to continue |
The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford had a three-run triple and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home — their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
PIRATES 4, ROYALS 3
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Rafael Flores Jr. hit the go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to help Pittsburgh to a win over Kansas City and complete a series sweep.
After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

Trea Turner News: On base four times in Saturday's loss
Turner went 2-for-3 with two walks, a run scored and a stolen base in Saturday's 10-3 loss to the Mets.
The star shortstop was busy on the basepaths Saturday, but Turner is struggling to build any momentum ahead of the playoffs. He's collected multiple hits in four of his last 11 games, but over that stretch he's batting just .256 (11-for-43) with two homers, three steals, five RBI and eight runs. Turner needs one more homer to record the fourth 20-20 campaign of his career.

item.content:encoded:
The Mets (70-84) defeated the Philadelphia Phillies (85-69) by a score of 6-3.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Mets left-handed starter Zac Thornton plunked leadoff batter Kyle Schwarber on a 3-2 count to get the game started. The rookie battled back, striking out Trea Turner and Bryce Harper before Mets first baseman Brett Baty made a diving stop on a Luis Arraez grounder down the line to put away the third out.
-- Southpaw Tim Mayza served as the bullpen opener for Philadelphia, and Francisco Lindor jumped all over him with a leadoff double. With one out, Bo Bichette worked a 10-pitch at-bat, culminating in a single to center field which moved Lindor up to third base. Carson Benge kept the line moving and drove in Lindor with an opposite-field single. Mark Vientos was walked to load the bases, and Phillies manager Don Mattingly pulled Mayza for right-handed reliever Jose Urquidy. A.J. Ewing roped an Urquidy fastball for a double, which scored two runs. Urquidy retired the next two Mets batters to limit the damage to three runs.
-- In the second inning, Ewing got turned around on a deep line drive to center, failing to haul in the RBI double for Bryson Stott, which cut the Mets' lead to 3-1. In the bottom half of the inning, Juan Soto doubled into the left-center field gap with two outs, but Urquidy struck out Bichette to end the threat.
-- With two outs away in the top of the sixth, Phillies left fielder Edmundo Sosa blasted a solo shot to left field, his third hit of the night. Excluding Sosa, Thornton allowed just two hits. He struck out four and walked one, allowing two earned runs across 87 pitches.
-- Soto took a hanging breaking ball thrown by Phillies right-hander Orion Kerkering 428 feet for a two-out three-run homer in the bottom of the sixth. Soto's 26th tater of 2026 put the Mets up 6-2.
-- Philadelphia center fielder Derek Hill responded with a solo home run off of Mets left-handed reliever Nate Lavender in the top of the seventh. Lavender persevered, retiring each of the next four batters he faced, before handing the ball to Dedniel Núñez to record the third out of the eighth. In the bottom half of the frame, Bichette grounded into a double play with the bases loaded. Núñez handled the ninth inning and retired the side to earn the first save of his season - and second save of his career - to seal the 6-3 win for the Mets.
Game MVP: Juan Soto
Soto notched his third game with multiple extra-base hits in September, going 3-for-5 with a double and a three-run homer. It was also Soto's third game of the season with at least three hits.
Highlights
What's next
The Mets play the Phillies in the third game of the four-game home series on Saturday at 4:10 p.m. on SNY. They will honor 2026 Baseball Hall of Fame inductee Carlos Beltrán.
New York will send out Christian Scott (3.76 ERA, 1.26 WHIP in 105.1 IP).
Philadelphia is set to start fellow right-hander Andrew Painter (5.54 ERA, 1.44 WHIP in 115.1 IP).
